chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Basir said:
I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who married four women in one contract and said in one session, and their dowries were different. He said: 'It is permissible for him and for them.'

I said: What do you think if he went to some lands, then divorced one of the four, and testified on her divorce with men from that land who did not know the woman? Then he married a woman from that land after the completion of the waiting period of the one he divorced, then died after consummating the marriage with her. How is his inheritance divided?

He said: 'If he has a son, then the woman whom he married last from the people of that land gets one-fourth of one-eighth of what he left. And if the one who was divorced from the four is known by her identity and lineage, then she gets nothing from the inheritance, and there is no waiting period upon her.'

He said: 'And the three women divide three-quarters of one-eighth of what he left among them all, and the waiting period is upon them. And if the one who was divorced from the four is not known, the four women divide three-quarters of one-eighth of what he left among them all, and the waiting period is upon them all.'
ai.seo_question: How is inheritance divided when a man divorces one of four wives in a single contract and then marries another before dying?
ai.summary: Abu Basir narrates this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), illustrating the practical application of polygyny and inheritance laws in early Shia jurisprudence. The Imam clarifies that if the divorced wife is identified, she receives no share and is exempt from iddah, whereas the new wife receives a reduced portion (one-eighth) due to the complexity of multiple concurrent marriages. This highlights the Shia emphasis on precise identification of spouses in inheritance distribution to avoid ambiguity.
